Title: The Case for Full Decriminalization of Consensual Adult Relationships Between Closely Related Individuals

Introduction
In a society that champions individual freedom and autonomy, the criminalization of private, consensual relationships between closely related adults stands as a troubling contradiction. This essay argues strongly for the full decriminalization of such intimate relationships, rooted in the radical principles of individual autonomy, adult consent, and personal liberty. Just as progressive societies have dismantled laws regulating non-heteronormative relationships and interracial marriages, we must now confront the outdated and intrusive nature of legal prohibitions against autonomy in such intensely personal matters. The state has no legitimate basis to penalize consenting adults for their intimate choices when harm to others cannot be demonstrated. Let’s explore why decriminalization aligns with ethical liberalism and reinforces the sanctity of self-determination.

1. Individual Autonomy: The Sovereignty of Self-Ownership

At its core, individual autonomy—the right to govern one’s own life—is the cornerstone of a free society. The philosopher John Stuart Mill articulated this beautifully in On Liberty, asserting that “over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign.” This sovereignty implies that individuals, not the state, should control decisions about their personal relationships. Prohibiting consensual relationships between cousins or siblings is akin to legalizing thought crimes: it penalizes intimate fellowship without addressing harm to others. To suggest the state knows better who we should love infringes on a fundamental human freedom, one that societies have historically expanded for other marginalized groups, such as LGBTQ+ individuals.

2. Adult Consent: The Non-Negotiable Boundary

Consent is the bedrock of any ethical legal system. Adults, by definition, possess the capacity to weigh risks and make decisions for themselves. When both parties are of age and freely agree, their private choices should not invite legal scrutiny. Opponents may cite risks like incest’s genetic consequences, but relinquishing autonomy to protect individuals from self-inflicted harm sets a dangerous precedent. We do not criminalize risky health behaviors like smoking or skydiving, even though they carry mortality risks. Similarly, the state has no authority to dictate private pleasures under the guise of paternalistic “protection.”

3. Reining in State Overreach: Privacy as a Liberty Issue

Government intrusion into bedroom choices erodes the very notion of a free society. Laws against consensual incest echo past moral crusades—laws banning interracial marriage or sodomy—that history has rightly condemned as violations of liberty. In Loving v. Virginia, the Supreme Court upheld marriage as a “basic civil right” and condemned miscegenation laws as “designed to maintain White supremacy.” Similarly, the Lawrence v. Texas ruling struck down anti-sodomy laws, affirming that moral disapproval alone cannot justify legal bans. The state’s role must remain confined to preventing harm, not policing taboo.

4. Genetic Concerns? Let Individuals Decide

Critics frequently cite genetic risks as justification, but these concerns misapply science to justify moralistic legislation. While studies suggest higher risks of genetic disorders in offspring, such outcomes are not guaranteed. Moreover, couples have the right to reproduce—or not—based on their own judgments, as in decisions about birth control or in vitro fertilization. Legal bans conflate physical intimacy with procreation, which are distinct choices. Even if reproduction is intended, the rights of prospective parents to make such decisions cannot be surrendered to the state in the name of “eugenics,” a practice with troubling historical ties to oppression.

5. The Tyranny of Majoritarian Morality

Opposition to such relationships often stems from disgust or cultural norms, not rational inquiry. Yet history reveals that societal discomfort is a flawed foundation for law. The abolition of countless obnoxious laws—from anti-sodomy statutes to Prohibition—proves that popular sentiment must not dictate civil rights. If legality depended on public tolerance, same-sex marriage or abortion rights might still be criminal. Decriminalization respects that morality cannot, and should not, be enforced through coercion.

6. Harm, the Ultimate Boundary

Mill’s “harm principle” insists the sole justification for limiting individual liberty is to prevent harm to others. Relationships between consenting adults cause no direct harm society can address. The act of intimacy is entirely private, and any indirect stigma is not sufficient grounds for prohibition. Even if one deems the relationships morally objectionable, one person’s moral disdain does not violate another person’s rights. The state has no obligation to enforce collective discomfort.

Conclusion
Criminalizing consensual relationships between closely related adults paints society as one that distrusts individuals to exercise their own judgment. By insisting on decriminalization, we reinforce the progressive ideal that adults should be free to live as they choose, provided they do not harm others. This stance honors the legacy of struggles against unjust moral legislation, from interracial marriage bans to anti-LGBTQ+ laws. A free people must reject legal overreach into private relationships, choosing instead to uphold the radical, enduring truths of autonomy and liberty. Let us not permit fear or taboos to corrode the principle that individuals, not the state, should chart their own lives.

Final Appeal
Decriminalization is not a call to endorse or celebrate such relationships, but a demand to honor the limits of law. In the words of Thomas Jefferson, “a wise and frugal government…shall restrain men from injuring one another, [but] shall leave them otherwise free to regulate their own pursuits of industry and improvement.” Let us choose wisdom, not fear. Let us choose liberty.

But two consenting adults who grew up sharing a towel and a microwave? Stop the presses. The heavens are weeping.

The “But What About the Children?!” Argument 💀

Ah yes, the classic “but what if they have babies!” panic.

First: babies are a choice. Not a biological inevitability. Also, 87% of people who have kids with their spouses do it without genetic screening—just by praying to the God of Spontaneous Ovulation and praying harder when the child has six toes.

Second: if we’re ruling out genetic risk, then we should also ban:

  • People over 40 from reproducing (They had three kids by 25! Pure chaos!)
  • Anyone who’s ever had secondhand smoke exposure (your lungs are contaminated, Jerry!)
  • Brits who drink tea with their eyes closed (we’ll never know what genetic mishaps are brewing!)

Also? You can get a DNA test. You can do IVF. You can use a surrogate named Bob who lives in Mexico and rides a Harley.

We’re not living in 1787—you don’t need to breed in a barn to make a baby. Technology exists. So does consent. And really, do you want to be the guy who stopped two people from getting married because they once shared a diaper? Because that’s the logic here.

A Modern Love Story (Real Life, I Swear)

Sophie and Caleb have been best friends since kindergarten. Last year, they realized they didn’t just share a childhood teddy bear... they also shared a love of vegan burritos, podcasting about tax law, and 7 a.m. hikes where they argue over whether pineapple belongs on pizza.

They kissed.

But the anti-incest lobby? They’re still posting:

Meanwhile, their dad just divorced their mom to marry his 19-year-old intern.
They named the kid “Joy.”
Joy is their half-sister.
Joy now calls Caleb “Uncle.”
Caleb is her biological uncle.
And because “someone has to”… Caleb now helps Joy with her algebra homework.

So, are we still against this? Or are we just confused?

CONCLUSION: WHERE IS THE LOGIC?

We live in a world where:

  • The President has a puppy named “Liberty” who votes in every election.
  • A woman legally married a famous internet meme of a cat.
  • There’s a cult in Oregon where people marry their WiFi router because “it connects me to the divine.”

But if two intelligent, loving, consenting adults who happen to have matching hairlines decide to build a life together… Suddenly it’s a national emergency?

To my fellow skeptics:

If your moral compass only points toward "eww," maybe it needs new batteries… or a therapist.

We should decriminalize adult consensual relationships—even if they share a last name.

Because love doesn’t care about genealogy.
Only bad Wi-Fi and awkward family reunions do.

And if you really think “incest” is the biggest threat to society...

...have you met Congress?
